## Course Overview

Welcome to this course on dynamic risk prediction. This course will provide an overview to principles of dynamic risk prediction. The course focuses on healthcare applications but many of the principles are more generally applicable.

&nbsp;
The figure below illustrates the course content, outlining the journey from data acquisition to the implementation of the final product.

<div style="overflow: auto; text-align: center;">
  <img src="../images/jouney_from_raw_to_implementation.PNG" alt="Image" style="margin-bottom: 15px; width: 85%;">
</div>

&nbsp;

The course is divided into four core modules, each covering a key stage, as illustrated in the figure above:

1) **Data Sources and Data Acquisition:**

This module a introduction to the data required for an dynamic risk prediction analysis is provided. Specifically, the definition of data, the characteristics of health data, potential issues associated with health data, and major data providers in Denmark are covered.

2) **Data Preprocessing:**

This module focuses on transforming raw health data into a clean, analysis-ready format. Common data challenges will be examined, and the reasons for data preprocessing will be explained. Furthermore, strategies for addressing the presented challenges while preparing the data for analysis will be discussed.

3) **Modeling:**

In this module, will guide through the process of building predictive models. It includes an introduction to both basic and advanced dynamic predictive models, such as logistic regression, decision trees, and recurrent neural networks. Topics include model performance metrics and hyperparameter tuning techniques.

4) **Implementation:**

The final module explores the challenges of implementing predictive tools in clinical settings. Topics include technical considerations such as system hosting and integration with live data sources, including an introduction to the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standard.

## Introduction to Dynamic Risk Prediction

Risk prediction is about estimating the probability of a binary future event or outcome for a patient. The estimation is typically based on a variety of variables, such as patient's characteristics, medical history and other relevant data.

Traditional risk prediction generates a risk estimate at specific time point in a patient’s disease trajectory, for example, the risk of death within 30 days following a surgical procedure. In contrast, dynamic risk prediction enables risk estimation at multiple time points throughout the disease course. The figure below illustrates the complex decision-making process that clinicians navigate during patient interactions, highlighting the critical questions they must address and how these considerations evolve throughout the patient's care timeline.

<div style="overflow: auto; text-align: center;">
  <img src="../images/dyn_pred_in_a_nutshell.PNG" alt="Image" style="margin-bottom: 15px; width: 75%;">
</div>

Dynamic risk prediction models are relevant because they can:

- continuously monitor changes in patient risk over time.
- inform timely interventions by providing insights that assist clinicians in making treatment decisions aligned with the patient’s current risk level.
- contribute to more efficient allocation of healthcare resources.

This course will present methodological and technical approaches for developing and implementing dynamic risk prediction models in healthcare, along with the associated challenges.

To describe dynamic risk prediction, there are the following elements:

- **A cohort of patients** with a clinical outcomes and relevant predictions recorded over time.
- **Prediction time points** $t_{ij}$ that denotes the specific time at which a prediction was made for the $i$'th patient at the $j$'th time point.
- **Binary outcome** $Y(t_{ij})$ for each prediction time $t_{ij}$, that a clinical outcome with only two possible values (e.g., positive or negative test, dead/alive).
- **Baseline data** $X_i$ for the $i$'th patient are characteristics that do not change over time, such as biological sex, age at diagnosis or genetic factors.
- **Time dependent data** $Z_i(t)$ for the $i$'th patient are measurements that vary over time, $t$, such as weight, laboratory values, or medication prescriptions.

The concept of multiple, irregular prediction times for a single patient is shown in the following illustration.

<div style="overflow: auto; text-align: center;">
  <img src="../images/Timeline_of_patients_visit.PNG" alt="Image" style="margin-bottom: 15px; width: 45%;">
</div>

## Example: 30-days Mortality in Advanced Lung Cancer

Patients suffering from cancer may receive systemic anti-cancer treatment (SACT) as a means of trying to influence disease progression, extend survival, and improve their quality of life.

While the intended outcomes of SACT can be beneficial, the treatment itself may also lead to serious adverse effect, even fatal ones. In the best-case scenario, particularly within palliative care, SACT can provide the highest possible quality of life alongside effective treatment outcomes. However, it can also result in increased suffering during a patient’s remaining lifetime. In the worst-case scenario, the overall outcome may be less favorable with SACT than without it, potentially leading to greater discomfort and even a shorter lifespan compared to supportive care alone.

To decide whether to initiate, continue or stop SACT is a complex and difficult decisions. To support this decision-making process, the development of dynamic predictive models is proposed as a valuable tool. These models could help clinicians make better-informed decisions about the optimal timing of SACT administration, or whether SACT is likely to do more harm than good in a particular patient's case. In a study by [Vesteghem et al.]((https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/CCI.22.00054?url_ver=Z39.88-2003&rfr_id=ori:rid:crossref.org&rfr_dat=cr_pub%20%200pubmed), they consider prediction of 30-days mortality among patients with advanced lung cancer. This was done dynamically, providing a new risk estimate each time the patient was in a drug administration event at the Dept. of Oncology. <!-- Correct the last sentence -->
